title: How to Hire Church Staff Well
subtitle: A practical guide to hiring church staff for character, fit, and calling, including the hard questions to ask before you put someone on the payroll of the body of Christ.

sections.title: Hire the Person, Not the Resume
sections.body:
The most impressive resume I ever read belonged to a man who nearly burned down a ministry. He could preach, he could administrate, he could fill a room. He also could not be told no, and within two years half the staff had quit and the rest were afraid of him. The resume was true. It was just measuring the wrong thing.

We hire for competence and fire for character, and we do it in that order almost every time. The skills are visible, easy to verify, easy to be dazzled by, and so they dominate the interview. Character is slow to see and easy to fake for an hour, so we skip it, and we pay for it for years. But Scripture never separates the two for those who lead in the church. The same qualifications that govern elders should govern anyone you pay to shepherd, because a staff member with a microphone has spiritual authority whether or not the title says so.

Not the most gifted candidate. The most trustworthy one. Gifting will draw a crowd, and character will be what determines whether that crowd is built up or used. When you cannot have both, take character, because you can grow a skill in a faithful person far more easily than you can grow faithfulness into a gifted one.

sections.title: Right Person, Wrong Church
sections.body:
Not every good candidate is a good fit, and confusing the two has wrecked more hires than outright bad character. A man can be godly, gifted, and genuinely called to ministry, and still be wrong for your church, and hiring him anyway is unkind to both of you.

Fit is the overlap between who they are and what this church actually is. A brilliant teacher who needs a study and a closed door will suffocate in a church that needs a pastor in the hospital at midnight. A high-energy planter who thrives on chaos will chafe in an established church that wants steady tending. Neither is a flaw in the person. It is a mismatch, and a mismatch sours into resentment on both sides. Ask not only is this person good but is this person good here, for these people, in this season.

This takes honesty about your own church most search teams cannot manage. We sell the candidate a church that does not exist, the one we wish we were, and then they arrive to find the real one and feel deceived. Tell the truth about who you are, the warts and the limits and the history, and let the right person choose you with their eyes open. A hire built on a sales pitch begins with a lie, and ministries built on lies do not last.

sections.title: The Questions Most Search Teams Are Too Polite to Ask
sections.body:
Most interviews are an exchange of pleasantries dressed as discernment. Tell us about your strengths. Where do you see yourself in five years. The candidate has rehearsed every answer, and the team learns nothing it could not have read on the resume. The questions that matter are the ones that make the room uncomfortable.

Ask about failure, and do not accept a humblebrag. Tell me about a time you sinned against someone on a staff and how it was resolved. Ask about money, plainly. Are you in debt, and how do you handle it. Ask about marriage, gently but really. How is your spouse, honestly, about this move. Ask about authority. Tell me about the last time you were told no by a supervisor and how you took it. Then call the references the candidate did not give you, because the ones they gave you were chosen to flatter, and the truth is usually one phone call to the side.

Watch what they do, not only what they say. How they treat the person who is not deciding, the assistant, the server at lunch, tells you more than an hour of answers. The hard questions feel rude. The alternative is hiring a stranger to shepherd souls because you were too polite to find out who they were. Be kind. Be thorough. Those are not opposites.

sections.title: Do Not Rush, and Do Not Stall
sections.body:
Two errors haunt church hiring, and they pull in opposite directions. We rush because the need is urgent, or we stall because the decision is hard, and both of them are failures of nerve.

The rush feels like faith and is often fear. The role is empty, the pressure is mounting, the obvious candidate is right there, and so we hire fast and call it providence. But a hasty hire is a slow disaster, and Paul warned Timothy against laying hands on anyone too quickly, lest he share in another man's sins. Take the time. Meet the family. Watch the candidate in unguarded moments. Let multiple people on your team weigh in, because the gift one person misses, another will catch. The stall is the opposite failure, the team so afraid of choosing wrong that it never chooses at all, leaving a ministry leaderless for a year while it waits for a certainty that does not exist this side of heaven.

Move deliberately and then decide. Bathe the whole thing in prayer, not as a formality but as the actual decision-maker, because you are choosing a shepherd for the flock of God and you cannot see the heart. He can. Ask him to. A church that hires on its knees will make fewer of the hires it spends years undoing.

sections.title: You Are Not Filling a Job
sections.body:
Somewhere in the hiring process it becomes a transaction. A position, a salary, a candidate, an offer, the same machinery any company runs. And the machinery is not wrong, but it hides the thing that is actually happening, and the thing that is actually happening is enormous.

You are entrusting souls to a person. You are putting someone in front of your children, beside your hurting, over your volunteers, into the pulpit or near it. The people of your church will follow this person, be shaped by this person, be wounded or healed by this person, for years after the interview is forgotten. That is not a hire. That is a stewardship, and you will answer for it as surely as the person you hire will answer for what they do with it.

I have hired in a hurry to relieve my own anxiety, and I have watched a church pay for my impatience long after my anxiety was gone. Treat the call as the sacred thing it is. You are not filling a vacancy on an org chart. You are placing a shepherd among sheep that belong to Christ, and the question that should govern the whole process is not can this person do the job. It is can I stand before God for having entrusted these people to this person. If you cannot answer that, you are not ready to make the offer.
